article.headline: AMD Earnings Jump 155.6% As Revenue Climbs 50.1% In June Quarter
article.deck: AMD is 4.0% past the 584.83 buy point of an 11-week cup and still inside a buy range that runs to 614.07.
body: Advanced Micro Devices designs the processors behind data centers and personal computers. Its line spans AI accelerators, microprocessors and graphics chips, along with embedded processors, programmable chips and custom system-on-chip work, sold through three segments: data center, client and gaming, and embedded.

The growth shows in the latest quarter. June-quarter earnings rose 155.6% to $1.38 a share, and revenue rose 50.1% to $11.54 billion. That followed earnings of 75 cents, 92 cents and 84 cents a share in the three quarters before, with revenue moving from $9.25 billion to $10.27 billion and $10.25 billion ahead of the jump. Earnings grew far faster than sales in the June quarter, which means each added dollar of revenue is carrying more profit. The next report is due Nov. 3, and it will show whether that pace held.

The market has paid up for that growth. AMD carries a $992.7 billion market value. It trades at 155.1 times trailing earnings and 38.7 times forward estimates, a gap that shows how much profit growth is already expected. Shares are up 183.9% this year and 158.2% over 12 months, and AMD ranks 97 of 99 on the desk's RS list.

The chart: AMD broke out Sept. 21 from an 11-week cup with a 584.83 buy point, on volume 1.88 times the 50-day average, the kind of turnout a breakout should bring. The cup corrected 27.5% from a June 30 high to a July 29 low of 424.03. Since the breakout the stock ran to a 52-week high of 658.52 and has pulled back. It closed Friday at 608.10, down 12.58, or 2.0%, which leaves it 4.0% above the buy point and inside the buy range that ends at 614.07.

Friday's decline came on volume 0.62 times average, a light pullback. The stock sits 7.7% below its high, 15.0% above its 50-day line at 528.92 and above the 21-day line at 595.08. The relative strength line is 6.3% off its high. Friday's low-volume dip kept the stock above the 21-day line, which is how a leader digests a run rather than how one breaks down.
Headlines Friday said tech rebounded as AI trade jitters eased, and TheStreet reported that CEO Su shared supply news with investors.

Fourteen sessions after the breakout, AMD is back in its buy range on light selling. The 21-day line is the first support on any further pullback; a close below 584.83 would turn the breakout into a failed one.
article.watch: The 21-day line at 595.08 and the Nov. 3 earnings report.

The relative strength line hit a new high, and the stock ranks 75 of 99 on the desk's RS list. Shares are 2.1% below the 52-week high of 61.14 and 6.6% above the 50-day line at 56.14, with the 21-day at 58.07. Exelixis is up 36.6% this year and 54.9% over 12 months.

June-quarter earnings rose 26.2% to 82 cents a share, and revenue rose 10.6% to $628.7 million. Revenue has increased in each quarter shown, from $597.8 million in the September 2025 quarter. The next report is due Oct. 27. The stock trades at 14.0 times forward earnings, with a $14.8 billion market value.
A Sept. 30 headline said Exelixis shares were rising on Cabometyx revenue. A Sept. 24 headline asked whether an FDA delay for zanzalintinib could affect the company's growth plans.
A close back under 59.82 would stall the breakout before it starts.
article.watch: Follow-through volume above the 50-day average, and the Oct. 27 earnings report.

market_note: The S&P 500 rose 0.6% to 7,811.54 and the Nasdaq gained 0.6% to 27,366.17, leaving them 1.5% and 3.0% above their 50-day lines, while the Dow rose 0.8% to 51,654.95 but stays 1.9% below its 50-day line. The S&P 500 carries seven distribution days over the last 25 sessions, the Dow six and the Nasdaq four, and the desk's state remains Market in correction. Software carried the day's breakouts, with Datadog, Palantir, Palo Alto Networks and Zeta Global past buy points alongside Arista, AbbVie and Exelixis, while the AI chip group keeps the list's highest average RS at 84 even as SanDisk, Arm, Lam Research and Astera Labs sit 7.0% to 13.5% below their buy points. No name on the desk's list moved 3% or more after hours.

corner.topic: How to buy a breakout: the buy point, the 5% buy range, and why volume has to confirm it
corner.headline: How To Buy A Breakout: Buy Point, Buy Range And Volume
corner.deck: Palo Alto Networks' cup shows all three parts of the rule, and the one it missed.
body: A breakout has three parts. There is the buy point, the price where the stock clears the top of its base. There is the buy range, which runs 5% above that buy point. And there is volume, which has to show that big investors are doing the buying. Miss any one and the odds turn against the trade.

The buy point comes from the base itself: take the high of the base and add ten cents. Palo Alto Networks built a seven-week cup that peaked Aug. 13 at 398.88, corrected 19.4% to a Sept. 2 low of 321.39 and climbed back up the right side. The buy point: 398.98.

The buy range caps what you pay. Five percent past 398.98 is 418.93, the top of the range. Buying inside it keeps the purchase close enough to the base that a normal shakeout does not force a sale. Buying above it is chasing: the stock has already made its move, and an ordinary pullback can erase the gain. On Friday Palo Alto rose 5.1% to 418.78, 5.0% above the buy point and right at the top edge of the range. Five sessions after the breakout, the entry is nearly gone.

Volume is the part most often skipped, and it is where Palo Alto falls short. A proper breakout comes on volume well above the 50-day average, the sign that funds are buying in size. Palo Alto broke out Oct. 2 on volume 0.79 times its 50-day average, below an ordinary day. Friday's 5.1% gain came on 0.63 times average. The price is up, but the heavy demand that confirms a breakout never showed on the chart.

What goes wrong without the rule? A buyer who ignores volume treats Palo Alto's light breakout the same as one backed by heavy institutional demand. A buyer who ignores the buy range and buys after Friday's jump pays near 418.93 instead of near 398.98, with almost no cushion above the base. If the breakout fails and the stock sinks back under 398.98, the late buyer takes the bigger loss.

The chart has strengths. Palo Alto's RS line is 0.2% from its high, the stock ranks 94 of 99 on the desk's RS list, and revenue rose 34.4% in the July quarter. But the rule is about the entry, and this entry was thin on volume and is now nearly used up. A buyer who missed it waits for a pullback to a moving average, such as the 21-day line at 389.84, or for a new base.
takeaways: The buy point is the base's high plus ten cents; for Palo Alto, 398.98.
The buy range ends 5% above the buy point; for Palo Alto, 418.93.
A breakout needs volume well above the 50-day average; Palo Alto's came at 0.79 times.
Past the top of the buy range, the entry is gone until a pullback or a new base.
Read the volume bar under the price bar before trusting a breakout.
